claims.text: The initial Mg-bearing lightweight high-entropy alloy contains a non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution.
Thermal exposure transforms the metastable solid solution.
The transformation precipitates Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
The transformation proceeds by a kinetically controlled nucleation-and-growth pathway.
Moderate aging below about 400 °C produces a fine, coherent dispersion of Mg-rich intermetallic nanoprecipitates.
Aging above about 700 °C or prolonged overaging produces coarser, contiguous intermetallic networks.
Fine, coherent intermetallic precipitates limit rapid internal diffusion.
Fine precipitates maintain beneficial partitioning of passivating elements.
Beneficial element partitioning can promote formation of stable oxide or passivation layers.
A fine precipitate dispersion retains corrosion resistance with minimal loss relative to the as-cast state.
A fine precipitate dispersion retains high-temperature oxidation resistance with minimal loss relative to the as-cast state.
Continuous intermetallic networks create preferential paths for oxidation.
Continuous intermetallic networks create preferential sites or paths for localized corrosion.
Coarse, continuous intermetallic networks degrade corrosion resistance.
Coarse, continuous intermetallic networks degrade high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Below about 400 °C, limited transformation kinetics favor formation or retention of fine nanoprecipitates.
Above about 700 °C, enhanced kinetics drive precipitate coarsening and formation of continuous intermetallic phases.
Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have a tendency to develop intermetallic compounds.
The as-cast metastable state exhibits initial corrosion resistance.
The as-cast metastable state exhibits initial high-temperature oxidation resistance.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome says moderate aging should cause minimal loss of corrosion and oxidation resistance relative to the as-cast state, whereas the falsification rule says that observing no significant performance difference from the as-cast state would falsify the mechanism. No significant difference is consistent with, rather than contrary to, the stated prediction.
